summary: At 41 people per square mile across 4,483 square miles of Sonoran Desert floor, Imperial County is one of the most sparsely populated places in California — roughly the size of Connecticut but with fewer residents than a mid-sized suburb. The landscape is almost aggressively flat: irrigated farmland fed by the Colorado River and the All-American Canal gives way to raw desert scrub, with the Salton Sea shimmering to the north and the Algodones Dunes — the largest sand dune system in North America — rolling along the eastern edge. Agriculture dominates the economy alongside government and healthcare jobs tied to the county's two major hospitals and proximity to the U.S.-Mexico border, where cross-border commerce through Calexico is a significant economic engine. Housing is strikingly affordable by California standards — a median home value of $279,500 against a median household income of $56,393 produces a price-to-income ratio under 5:1, a number most coastal Californians would find surreal — though a 19.6% poverty rate signals that affordability here reflects constrained wages more than hidden bargains. With an average daily high of 87°F year-round and 10.6 hours of sunshine per day, summers regularly push past 110°F, making outdoor life genuinely seasonal. Imperial is a place where the economics of California finally make numerical sense, but the desert collects its own kind of rent.
